content: Healthcare in India is primarily the responsibility of individual Indian states. The Indian Constitution mandates these states to focus on improving public health, raising nutritional levels, and enhancing the standard of living for their populations. A National Health Policy, first endorsed by Parliament in 1983, also guides healthcare efforts. Critics argue that the National Health Policy lacks specific measures to achieve its broad goals. Key issues include the failure to integrate health services with broader economic and social development, insufficient nutritional support and sanitation, and inadequate local-level participatory involvement. The central government has attempted to influence public health through five-year plans, coordinated planning with states, and sponsorship of major health programs. Funding for healthcare is shared between the central and state governments, with goals and strategies determined through consultations between the two levels of government via the Central Council of Health and Family Welfare. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare oversees central government efforts, providing administrative and technical services and managing medical education, while states are responsible for public services and health education. The 1983 National Health Policy aimed to provide universal health services by the year 2000. However, healthcare expenditures varied significantly among states and union territories. For example, in 1983, per capita spending ranged from Rs 13 in Bihar to Rs 60 in Himachal Pradesh. India's per capita healthcare expenditure was low compared to other Asian countries outside South Asia. Although government healthcare spending increased during the 1980s, it remained relatively constant as a percentage of GDP and decreased as a share of total government spending. By the mid-1990s, health spending accounted for 6% of GDP, one of the highest levels among developing nations. Per capita spending was approximately Rs 320 annually, with private households contributing 75% of the total expenditure. A 1995 World Bank study revealed that 8% of spending went to secondary and tertiary inpatient care, while the remainder was allocated to non-service costs. The fifth and sixth five-year plans (FY 1974–78 and FY 1980–84) included programs to deliver preventive medicine and improve rural health. High priorities included supplemental nutrition programs and increasing access to safe drinking water. The sixth plan also emphasized training community health workers and controlling communicable diseases, while addressing regional imbalances in healthcare resource distribution. Primary healthcare facilities and personnel expanded significantly between the early 1950s and 1980s. However, rapid population growth led to a decline in the number of licensed medical practitioners per 10,000 individuals, from four in 1981 to three by the late 1980s. In 1991, there were approximately ten hospital beds per 10,000 individuals. Primary health centers (PHCs) are the cornerstone of rural healthcare, with around 22,400 PHCs, 11,200 hospitals, and 27,400 dispensaries in operation by 1991. These facilities are part of a tiered healthcare system that directs complex cases to urban hospitals while providing routine care to rural populations. PHCs and sub-centers rely on trained paramedics to meet most healthcare needs. Challenges for PHCs include a focus on clinical and curative care over preventive work and staff reluctance to work in rural areas. Additionally, the integration of health services with family planning programs often leads to local populations perceiving PHCs as antagonistic to their preference for larger families. This perception can hinder the implementation of national health policies at the local level. In 1989, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare reported a total of 10,157 civilian hospitals across all states and union territories. By 1991, there were 811,000 hospital and healthcare facility beds. The distribution of hospitals varied based on local socio-economic conditions. For instance, Uttar Pradesh, with a 1991 population exceeding 139 million, had 735 hospitals in 1990, while Kerala, with a population of 29 million, had 2,053 hospitals. Despite the central government's goal of universal healthcare by 2000, hospitals were unevenly distributed. Private studies in the early 1990s estimated a total of 7,300 hospitals in 1992, with nearly 4,000 owned and managed by government entities, 2,000 by charitable trusts (partially supported by the government), and 1,300 by the private sector. Many private hospitals lacked advanced medical facilities, though approximately 12% had state-of-the-art equipment for diagnosing and treating major diseases, including cancer. The rapid growth of the private medical sector and the expanding middle class in the 1990s introduced the concept of for-profit hospitals and healthcare facilities in India. By the late 1980s, there were approximately 128 medical colleges, three times the number in 1950. In 1987, these colleges admitted a combined annual class of 14,166 students. Data from 1987 indicated 320,000 registered medical practitioners and 219,300 registered nurses. Studies have shown that both urban and rural populations preferred paying for private healthcare services over using free public health centers. Indigenous or traditional medical practitioners continue to operate throughout the country. The two main traditional systems are Ayurveda, which addresses mental, spiritual, and physical well-being, and Unani (or Galenic) herbal medicine. Practitioners of Ayurveda are called vaidyas, while Unani practitioners are known as hakims. These professions are often hereditary, and various institutions provide training in indigenous medical practices. Official health policy only began to reference integration between Western-oriented medical personnel and indigenous practitioners in the late 1970s. By the early 1990s, there were 98 Ayurvedic colleges and 17 Unani colleges operating in both governmental and non-governmental sectors.
